note: Fixtures are described in `fixture` and not shipped, so build each one as a small folder before the run. The plugin's PreToolUse hook makes Claude load the skill before its first .tex edit, and its description triggers it for Quarto and Markdown notes and chat replies. Each eval tests what the rules change, and its assertions are checked on the edited files and the transcript.

evals.name: restructure-lasso-theorem
evals.prompt: clean up the statement of theorem 2 in theory/lasso-rate.tex
evals.fixture: paper/ on high-dimensional regression, with main.tex, sections/10-introduction.tex and theory/lasso-rate.tex. The introduction says the paper's contribution is to show how the restricted eigenvalue constant drives the lasso error. sections/20-setup.tex defines the design matrix X with n rows and p columns, the true coefficient vector \beta^*, its support S with s = |S|, and the noise vector. Theorem 2 reads, in one paragraph: 'Let \hat\beta be the lasso estimate with \lambda = 2\sigma\sqrt{2\log(2p)/n}, where the noise is sub-Gaussian with parameter \sigma. Suppose the columns of X are normalized, \beta^* is s-sparse, and X satisfies the restricted eigenvalue condition over S with constant \kappa > 0. Then \|\hat\beta - \beta^*\|_2 \le C \sigma \sqrt{s \log p / n} / \kappa with probability at least 1 - 1/p (in fact C = 3 works, and sub-Gaussian noise can be relaxed to finite fourth moments at the cost of a log factor). If, in addition, \min_{j \in S} |\beta^*_j| > 2 C \sigma \sqrt{s \log p / n} / \kappa, the lasso recovers S.' The proof in the same file uses every condition in the statement.
evals.expected_output: Moves the sub-Gaussian noise condition out of the Let part, so that the Let part only names the lasso estimate and its tuning parameter. Puts the regularity conditions, such as sub-Gaussian noise and normalized columns, inline in a Suppose that part. Treats the restricted eigenvalue condition as substantive, given the introduction, and puts it in an If part. Displays the error bound in the Then part. Says what the constant C depends on, or states its value, and keeps the probability statement. Moves the remarks about C = 3 and about fourth moments to a paragraph after the statement. Turns the support-recovery sentence into a corollary that starts 'Assume the conditions of' Theorem 2, cited with \cref.
assertions: The Let part of the rewritten theorem imposes no condition on the noise
Sub-Gaussian noise and normalized columns are in a Suppose that part, written inline and not as display equations
The restricted eigenvalue condition is in an If part
The error bound on \|\hat\beta - \beta^*\|_2 is a display equation
The statement says what C depends on or gives its value, and keeps the probability at least 1 - 1/p
The remarks about C = 3 and about finite fourth moments are not inside the theorem environment and appear in a paragraph after it
The support-recovery claim is a separate corollary that starts with 'Assume the conditions of' and cites Theorem 2 with \cref, and no sentence starts with 'If, in addition'

evals.name: lemma-in-quarto-note
evals.prompt: in notes/sample-split.qmd, state the lemma we used to kill the empirical process term, right before the step that uses it
evals.fixture: a Quarto project whose notes/sample-split.qmd holds a derivation in Quarto's $...$ math. It defines the empirical measure P_n of n observations, the true distribution P, a fixed function f_0 and an estimate \hat f that is fit on a second sample independent of the n observations. One step of the derivation says '(P_n - P)(\hat f - f_0) = o_P(n^{-1/2}) by sample splitting and Chebyshev' with no stated lemma. The note has no .tex file and no lemma environments.
evals.expected_output: Writes the lemma in Quarto syntax, before the step that uses it. The Let part names \hat f as an estimate fit on an independent sample, with no further condition on it. A Suppose that part states boundedness or a second-moment condition inline. The If part states \|\hat f - f_0\|_{L_2(P)} = o_P(1). The Then part displays (P_n - P)(\hat f - f_0) = o_P(n^{-1/2}) and says that the order is in probability as n grows. The statement has no symbol that only the proof uses, such as a conditional variance, and no commentary. The derivation step then cites the lemma.
assertions: The lemma is written in Quarto math syntax in notes/sample-split.qmd and placed before the step that uses it
The lemma has a Let part, a Suppose that or If part, and a Then part, in that order
The L2 consistency of \hat f is in the If part, not in the Let part
The conclusion (P_n - P)(\hat f - f_0) = o_P(n^{-1/2}) is a display equation
The statement defines no symbol that only the proof uses
The step of the derivation that used 'sample splitting and Chebyshev' now refers to the lemma

evals.name: corollary-not-in-addition
evals.prompt: add to theorem 1 that the estimator is efficient when the outcome regression is correctly specified
evals.fixture: paper/ on a regression-adjusted estimator in randomized trials. theory/adjusted-normal.tex holds Theorem 1, with \label{thm:adjusted-normal}, which states asymptotic normality of the estimator \hat\tau with an asymptotic variance V given in a display, under bounded outcomes and a known randomization probability. sections/20-setup.tex defines the efficiency bound V^* in a labelled equation, eq:bound.
evals.expected_output: Leaves the statement of Theorem 1 unchanged. Adds a corollary after it, in its own file or in the same theory file as the paper's layout requires, that starts 'Assume the conditions of \cref{thm:adjusted-normal} hold.', then says 'If' the outcome regression is correctly specified, 'then' V = V^*, with V = V^* displayed. Adds a short paragraph after the corollary that says what it means.
assertions: The statement of Theorem 1 is unchanged
No sentence in the new text starts with 'If, in addition'
A new corollary starts with 'Assume the conditions of' and cites Theorem 1 with \cref
The correct specification of the outcome regression is in the corollary's If part
The conclusion that the asymptotic variance equals the efficiency bound is a display equation

evals.name: note-names-add-and-subtract
evals.prompt: in notes/one-step.tex, pick up after the von Mises expansion and show that the one-step estimator is asymptotically linear
evals.fixture: notes/one-step.tex, a standalone note that no paper inputs, whose first line is the mode line % writing-math: note, semiparametric statistics; refs: van der Vaart 1998. It defines the data O = (X, A, Y) from P_0, the target \psi(P) = E_P[\mu_P(1, X)] with efficient influence function \varphi_P, an initial estimate \hat P of P_0 with \hat\varphi = \varphi_{\hat P}, and the one-step estimator \hat\psi = \psi(\hat P) + P_n \hat\varphi. It ends with the von Mises expansion \psi(\hat P) - \psi(P_0) = -P_0 \hat\varphi + R_2(\hat P, P_0), which defines the remainder R_2.
evals.expected_output: Writes \hat\psi - \psi(P_0) = (P_n - P_0)\hat\varphi + R_2 in short steps from the definition of the one-step estimator and the expansion. Then adds and subtracts (P_n - P_0)\varphi_0, names that step, and says that it isolates the term to which the central limit theorem applies. For the result that makes the empirical process term (P_n - P_0)(\hat\varphi - \varphi_0) of order o_P(n^{-1/2}), either cites it by name and number from van der Vaart (1998), such as the Donsker-class lemma, or restates it as a lemma, such as a sample-splitting argument through Chebyshev's inequality, and checks its conditions or adds them as assumptions. States the condition that makes R_2 of order o_P(n^{-1/2}) instead of asserting the order. No line of the derivation jumps more than two or three elementary moves, and no 'clearly' or 'it follows' stands without the steps that show why.
assertions: Names the add-and-subtract step that splits (P_n - P_0)\hat\varphi into (P_n - P_0)\varphi_0 and (P_n - P_0)(\hat\varphi - \varphi_0), or an equivalent step, and says what it is for

Cites the result that makes (P_n - P_0)(\hat\varphi - \varphi_0) = o_P(n^{-1/2}) by name and number from van der Vaart (1998), or restates it as a lemma with its conditions, for example sample splitting with L2(P_0) consistency of \hat\varphi
Checks the conditions of that result where the note applies it, or adds them to the note as assumptions
States the condition under which R_2 = o_P(n^{-1/2}), such as a product-rate condition on the nuisance errors, and does not assert the order without it
Makes at most two or three elementary moves between any two consecutive lines of the derivation
Uses 'clearly', 'it follows', 'after some algebra' or a similar phrase only where the text around it shows why

evals.name: root-file-without-mode-line
evals.prompt: add a remark after theorem 2 on why the product rate condition is needed and when it holds
evals.fixture: paper/ folder of a paper on cross-fitted TMLE. main.tex has no % writing-math: line and inputs sections/10-introduction.tex to sections/50-discussion.tex. sections/20-setup.tex defines the propensity score \pi_0 and the outcome regression \mu_0. Theorem 2 in sections/40-theory.tex assumes \|\hat\pi - \pi_0\| \|\hat\mu - \mu_0\| = o_P(n^{-1/2}), with norms in L2(P_0). The text is at one sentence per line.
evals.expected_output: Sees that the root file main.tex has no mode line. Chooses paper mode, since the remark goes in the main text of the paper, a field from the content, such as semiparametric statistics, and two to four reference texts that readers in that field know, such as van der Vaart (1998). Adds % writing-math: paper, <field>; refs: <texts> near the top of main.tex, and tells the user which mode, field and texts it chose, so that they can change the line. Writes the remark in sections/40-theory.tex at the density of a paper in that field.
assertions: Adds a comment line of the form % writing-math: paper, <field>; refs: <texts> near the top of paper/main.tex
Puts the mode line in the root file main.tex and not in a section file
Chooses paper mode and a field that fits the paper, such as semiparametric statistics, causal inference or asymptotic statistics
Names two to four reference texts that readers in that field know well
Tells the user which mode, field and reference texts it chose, and that they can change the line

evals.name: note-optimum-in-full
evals.prompt: in notes/allocation.tex, work out the treated fraction that minimizes the variance of the difference in means, given that at most 70% of the units can be treated
evals.fixture: notes/allocation.tex, a standalone note whose first line is the mode line % writing-math: note, design of experiments; refs: Imbens and Rubin 2015. It defines n units, the treated fraction p, the outcome standard deviations \sigma_1 and \sigma_0 in the treated and the control arm, and the difference-in-means estimator \hat\tau.
evals.expected_output: Writes the variance of \hat\tau as the function \sigma_1^2/(np) + \sigma_0^2/(n(1-p)) of p, and states the feasible region 0 < p \le 0.7. Gives the reason for the direction of monotonicity, from the sign of the derivative on each side of the stationary point or from convexity. Derives the unconstrained minimizer p = \sigma_1/(\sigma_1 + \sigma_0) from the first-order condition. Treats both cases of the cap: that minimizer when it is at most 0.7, and p = 0.7 when \sigma_1 > (7/3)\sigma_0, where the variance decreases on the whole feasible region. Makes at most two or three elementary moves per line, and puts each new sentence on its own line.
assertions: Writes the variance of the difference in means as a function of the treated fraction p
States the feasible region of p, 0 < p \le 0.7
Gives the reason for the direction of monotonicity, such as the sign of the derivative on each side of the stationary point, or convexity
Derives the unconstrained minimizer \sigma_1/(\sigma_1 + \sigma_0) from the first-order condition, and does not only assert it
Treats both cases of the cap: the minimizer when \sigma_1/(\sigma_1 + \sigma_0) \le 0.7, and p = 0.7 otherwise, which happens when \sigma_1 > (7/3)\sigma_0
Shows why the cap binds in the second case, because the variance decreases on the whole feasible region, and does not only say that it binds
Makes at most two or three elementary moves between any two consecutive lines of the derivation

evals.name: restate-result-from-paper
evals.prompt: finish the proof of theorem 3 with the oracle inequality from Lee and Park (2021)
evals.fixture: paper/ on nonparametric regression, whose main.tex has the mode line % writing-math: paper, nonparametric statistics; refs: Wainwright 2019, Tsybakov 2009. sections/20-setup.tex defines the regression function f_0, the function class \mathcal{F}, the squared-loss estimator \hat f and the empirical norm. theory/rate.tex holds Theorem 3, a rate for \|\hat f - f_0\|_n, with a proof that stops at the step that needs an oracle inequality and, later, a tail bound for a sum of bounded independent terms. refs/lee-park-2021.pdf is the paper; its Theorem 4 is an oracle inequality for a general loss \ell over a star-shaped class G, under its conditions (L1) to (L3), in its own notation.
evals.expected_output: Reads Theorem 4 in refs/lee-park-2021.pdf. Adds a lemma that restates it for the paper's setting: the squared loss, the class \mathcal{F} and the empirical norm, in the paper's notation, with (L1) to (L3) written as conditions on the paper's objects, and the citation 'Lee and Park (2021, Theorem 4)'. Says in a sentence how the general theorem gives this special case. Checks each condition of the lemma where the proof applies it. For the tail bound, cites Hoeffding's or Bernstein's inequality by name and number from Wainwright (2019) and does not prove or restate it. Names the conditions and the lemma that each step of the proof uses.
assertions: Adds a lemma that states the oracle inequality in the paper's notation, for the squared loss and the class \mathcal{F}, not in the general notation of Lee and Park
The lemma cites the exact theorem, Lee and Park (2021, Theorem 4)
The lemma's conditions are written as conditions on the paper's objects, and none of (L1) to (L3) is dropped without a reason
A sentence says how the general theorem of Lee and Park gives the lemma
The proof cites the tail bound by name and by a theorem or proposition number in Wainwright (2019), and does not prove or restate it
Each step of the proof that uses the new lemma or a condition names it

evals.name: long-appendix-proof-numbered-steps
evals.prompt: rewrite the proof of lemma B.2 so it follows our proof rules
evals.fixture: paper/ on kernel density estimation, whose main.tex has the mode line % writing-math: paper, nonparametric statistics; refs: Tsybakov 2009, Giné and Nickl 2016. theory/uniform-rate.tex holds Lemma B.2, a uniform rate for the kernel density estimator under the labelled conditions (Bounded kernel), (Bandwidth) and (Smooth density), and its proof, which proof-at-the-end prints in the appendix and which runs to about two pages of prose. The proof says 'by assumption' three times without saying which condition. It proves Markov's inequality in full in one paragraph, and passes over the step that bounds the supremum of the empirical process with the one sentence 'a standard chaining argument gives the bound'. One of its claims is stated first and followed by 'To see this, ...'. Its last part argues by contradiction but never uses the negated assumption. The proof uses every condition of the lemma.
evals.expected_output: Keeps the statement of Lemma B.2. Writes the proof as numbered steps, each a claim with a short proof under it, with sub-steps where a proof needs more detail, and a last step that concludes. Starts with a sentence or two of plan that says which step is the key one, the bound on the supremum. Replaces each 'by assumption' with the label of the condition used. Cites Markov's inequality by name and does not prove it. Writes out the chaining step, or cites the chaining bound by name and number from Giné and Nickl (2016) and checks its conditions. States each claim as the step itself instead of 'To see this'. Rewrites the spurious proof by contradiction as a direct argument.
assertions: The proof is written as numbered steps in an enumerate list, each step a claim followed by its proof
A plan of one or two sentences before the steps names the key step
No step says 'by assumption' without the label of the condition it uses
Markov's inequality is cited by name and not proved
The chaining step is written out, or the chaining bound is cited by name and number from Giné and Nickl (2016) with its conditions checked
The part that argued by contradiction is now a direct argument
The statement of Lemma B.2 is unchanged
